intro: Chopin’s Étude in G♭ major, Op. 25 No. 9, known as the Butterfly, is a quick study built on groups of four notes, a leap followed by two short octaves. Edward Neeman plays it in this recording for Musopen.

sections.label: A · Octaves in G♭ major
sections.mNote: Four semiquavers to each beat, with sharply contrasted touches.

sections.label: B · Octaves over leaping bass
sections.mNote: The left hand alternates between bass notes and chords.

sections.label: C · Four-note figure continued
sections.mNote: Slurred pairs and detached octaves alternate throughout

sections.label: D · Closing section in G♭
sections.mNote: The right hand flies high above G♭-major chords

cues.title: Right-hand figuration, opening bars
cues.text: Each beat has four semiquavers. The first two are slurred and the next two are detached octaves, while the left hand leaps from a single bass note to a chord. Chopin marks the passage leggiero.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, opening bars: Allegro assai, leggiero, four-note right-hand groups and leaping left-hand quavers. Chopin Institute digital score: https://chopinscores.org/partytura/194
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Edward Neeman, ballet pianist
cues.text: Edward Neeman has also worked as a ballet pianist. In 2014 he accompanied American Ballet Theatre on its Japanese tour. He also plays in the Neeman Piano Duo with his wife, Stephanie.
cues.evidence: Australian National University biography of Edward Neeman documents the 2014 ballet tour and his duo with Stephanie Neeman: https://music.cass.anu.edu.au/people/dr-edward-neeman

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
